summary:
FireHarmonics is an independent research prototype for exploring cross-sensor harmonization of NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations. Using NASA FIRMS archive data, we built a unified dataset of 769,672 observations from five satellite platforms: Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21.

Our DORA (Detection Observation Relationship Analysis) workflow identifies potential cross-sensor observation relationships using spatial proximity, acquisition-time differences, matching dates, and day/night categories. It preserves multiple candidate relationships and evaluates how spatial and temporal thresholds affect the results, rather than forcing uncertain one-to-one matches.

An interactive Streamlit dashboard brings together multi-year activity analysis, sensor comparisons, anomaly screening, contextual HLS scene inventory, and a retrospective stakeholder review workflow.

FireHarmonics aims to make multi-sensor satellite observation analysis more transparent, reproducible, and uncertainty-aware. Candidate relationships are exploratory and are not confirmed physical fire matches or independently validated accuracy measurements.
details:
FireHarmonics: Uncertainty-Aware Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Active-Fire Observations

1. What We Built

FireHarmonics is an independent research prototype for cross-sensor harmonization and analysis of NASA MODIS and VIIRS active-fire satellite observations.

Different satellite instruments observe the Earth with different spatial, temporal, and sensor characteristics. These differences make direct comparisons challenging and can create ambiguity when observations from multiple platforms are analyzed together.

To explore this problem, we developed a unified multi-platform observation dataset and DORA (Detection Observation Relationship Analysis), a spatial-temporal candidate relationship analysis workflow.

Our objective is to make cross-sensor observation comparisons more transparent, reproducible, and uncertainty-aware.

2. NASA Data and Methodology

The project uses historical NASA FIRMS archive observations from five satellite platforms:

  • MODIS Aqua
  • MODIS Terra
  • VIIRS Suomi-NPP
  • VIIRS NOAA-20
  • VIIRS NOAA-21

The harmonized dataset covers 1 March 2023 to 31 July 2026.

First, observations are standardized into a common data structure while preserving their source identifiers, platform, sensor, timestamps, coordinates, and other available observation attributes. Unique observation identifiers and data-quality checks help maintain traceability throughout the analysis.

DORA then explores potential relationships between MODIS Aqua and VIIRS observations through:

  • Geographic proximity using Haversine distance calculations.
  • Acquisition-time differences.
  • Matching acquisition dates.
  • Consistent day/night observation categories.

The baseline exploratory configuration uses a 2 km spatial threshold and a 240-minute temporal window. Additional threshold analysis explores spatial thresholds of 1 km, 2 km, and 5 km and temporal windows of 60, 120, and 240 minutes.

Rather than automatically forcing every observation into a single match, DORA preserves multiple candidate relationships. This allows the workflow to expose ambiguity and examine how different analytical thresholds affect candidate relationships.

The analysis also documents observations outside the Aqua-primary comparison scope instead of silently discarding them.

3. Current Results and Evidence

The latest audited harmonized dataset contains:

  • 769,672 unique satellite observations.
  • Five satellite platforms across MODIS and VIIRS sensors.
  • A date range from 1 March 2023 to 31 July 2026.
  • Unique observation identifiers and validated coordinate and timestamp fields.

The optimized DORA workflow produced:

  • 311,918 spatial candidate records within the 5 km candidate-search scope.
  • 106,203 baseline candidate pairs using the 2 km and 240-minute criteria.
  • 718,804 observations in the audited Aqua-primary comparison scope.
  • 50,868 documented scope exclusions, with the input accounting reconciled.

Additional analytical components include:

Historical activity analysis: Multi-year daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly, seasonal, yearly, platform-level, sensor-level, day/night, hourly, and approximate 5 km spatial-grid summaries.

Sensor comparability analysis: Exploratory platform and sensor comparisons, confidence-category summaries, one-to-one baseline summaries, and date-cluster bootstrap analysis. These are exploratory comparisons, not independently established sensor accuracy or calibration results.

Historical anomaly screening: The workflow generated 2,610 anomaly alerts using a platform- and spatial-grid-based historical baseline. It uses the preceding 28-day active-observation history and requires at least seven prior active days. These alerts identify unusual observation activity, not confirmed fire outbreaks.

Critical observation activity windows: Analysis of the complete years 2024 and 2025 identified May and October–November as recurring high-observation activity windows under the project's defined metric. These are satellite-observation activity patterns, not independently confirmed fire seasons or causal risk forecasts.

NASA HLS L30 contextual inventory: We examined 36 sampled DORA candidate locations through NASA's Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 (HLS) catalogue. HLS scenes were found for 34 locations, and 30 priority scene records received asset-metadata review. The review confirmed the availability of Fmask and RGB asset references. Imagery was not downloaded for pixel-level validation.

All reported figures refer to the project's audited analytical outputs and their documented scopes.

4. Interactive Research Platform

We developed a Streamlit-based interactive dashboard that brings the project's analytical outputs together.

The platform includes:

  • Harmonized dataset and satellite-platform summaries.
  • DORA candidate relationship exploration.
  • Spatial and temporal threshold sensitivity analysis.
  • Observation ambiguity inspection.
  • Interactive geographic maps and visualizations.
  • Multi-year activity and sensor comparison analysis.
  • Historical anomaly screening.
  • NASA HLS scene-inventory context.
  • Retrospective stakeholder review workflow.
  • Data filtering and CSV exports.
  • Methodology explanations and scientific limitations.

A dedicated Research Explorer brings together the major analytical components so users can investigate the evidence without manually navigating multiple large CSV files.

The stakeholder workflow organizes historical anomaly records for analyst review. Its priority categories are review aids, not emergency classifications or live dispatch instructions.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The central creative contribution of FireHarmonics is its uncertainty-aware approach to cross-sensor observation harmonization.

Instead of treating every nearby MODIS and VIIRS observation as a confirmed one-to-one match, DORA models potential relationships and preserves competing candidates.

This enables users to:

  • Inspect multiple possible relationships.
  • Identify ambiguous observations.
  • Examine the effect of spatial and temporal thresholds.
  • Distinguish candidate relationships from confirmed matches.
  • Review documented exclusions and unmatched observations.
  • Understand the limitations of cross-sensor comparisons.

The project combines observation harmonization, historical activity analysis, exploratory sensor comparability, anomaly screening, contextual HLS metadata, and an interactive research interface in one reproducible workflow.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

FireHarmonics aims to support researchers, students, and people working with satellite-based fire observations.

Its potential benefits include:

  • More transparent comparisons between MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Better understanding of spatial and temporal differences between satellite platforms.
  • Identification of ambiguous candidate relationships.
  • Easier exploration of large multi-platform satellite datasets.
  • Reproducible analytical workflows with traceable data provenance.
  • A foundation for future validation using independent reference datasets.

In the longer term, uncertainty-aware multi-sensor analysis could contribute to research on satellite observation consistency and the development of more reliable fire-monitoring workflows.

FireHarmonics is a research and analysis prototype. It is not presented as an operational fire-alert service or a replacement for official emergency-monitoring systems.

7. Tools and Technologies

  • Programming language: Python
  • Data processing: Pandas and NumPy
  • Spatial analysis: Scikit-learn BallTree and Haversine distance calculations
  • Interactive dashboard: Streamlit
  • Visualization: Plotly and Folium
  • Primary satellite data source: NASA FIRMS historical archive
  • Contextual satellite data source: NASA HLS L30 catalogue and CMR-STAC
  • Data formats: CSV and JSON
  • Testing: Pytest
  • Development environment: Windows and Python virtual environment

The implementation uses software-based data processing and analysis and does not require specialized hardware.

8. Scientific Considerations and Limitations

Scientific transparency is an important part of FireHarmonics.

The project accounts for sensor differences, data provenance, spatial and temporal thresholds, day/night categories, candidate ambiguity, documented scope exclusions, and reproducibility checks.

However, several limitations must be considered:

  • A candidate relationship does not establish that two observations represent the same physical fire.
  • An unmatched observation does not establish that a satellite sensor missed a fire.
  • Candidate counts are not confirmed fire counts.
  • Candidate relationships and rankings are not probabilities of a correct match.
  • No independent ground-truth dataset has yet been used to establish matching accuracy.
  • Differences in native sensor confidence categories and FRP values do not independently establish calibration bias.
  • Historical anomaly alerts indicate unusual observation volume, not confirmed fire outbreaks.
  • Critical activity windows describe satellite-observation activity and do not establish causal fire risk or confirmed fire seasons.
  • The spatial grid is approximate and is not an equal-area grid.
  • NASA HLS scene metadata availability does not establish clear-pixel confirmation or thermal fire validation. No HLS imagery was downloaded for pixel-level validation.

The final release audit reported AUDIT_PASS_WITH_LIMITATIONS, with 56 automated tests passing. The dashboard was also manually launched and checked. These checks support implementation and reproducibility, but they do not constitute independent scientific validation.

FireHarmonics is an independent research prototype and does not imply NASA endorsement.

9. Super Intelligence (SI) Use Disclosure

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted development tool for ideation, research support, analytical interpretation, coding assistance, debugging, and documentation editing.

The project team reviewed and tested the implementation and remains responsible for the final work, its methodology, and its scientific claims.

The satellite observation data were sourced from NASA FIRMS and processed through the project's analytical workflows; they were not generated by AI.

No AI-generated NASA logos, mission identifiers, or NASA branding were used.
